arguments.title: What to note before you bring a bike in for a recurring flat tire
arguments.content:
A flat that keeps coming back is usually telling you something. The details you notice at home help our workshop find the cause faster, instead of repairing the same hole twice.

This post is a short preparation checklist. It covers what to observe, what to bring, and how to describe the problem when you drop the bike off for puncture repair.

Note how fast the air goes

Timing is the single most useful clue. Try to place your flat in one of these groups:

  • Air gone in seconds or a minute after inflating.
  • Soft after a few hours.
  • Soft after several days, but rideable in between.
  • Only flat after a specific ride or a specific route.

Write the answer down or note it in your phone. A slow weekly leak and a sudden blowout point at different parts of the wheel.

Note where the bike was when it happened

Record the last ride before the air loss. Useful details include the surface you rode on, whether you hit a kerb or pothole, and whether the bike sat outside in cold weather. If the flat appeared while the bike was parked and untouched, say that too. A leak with no ride attached often sits at the valve or the rim side of the tube rather than the tread.

Check the outside of the tire without taking it apart

You do not need to strip the wheel before your visit. A visual check is enough:

  • Look across the tread for cuts, embedded glass, thorns, or wire.
  • Look at the sidewalls for cracks, bulges, or worn patches.
  • Check whether the tread pattern is worn flat in the centre.
  • Look at the rim edge for dents or rough spots.

Leave anything you find in place if you can. An object still stuck in the tread shows us exactly where to inspect the tube.

Note what has already been repaired

Tell us the repair history of that wheel. Helpful points are how many times it has gone flat, whether patches were fitted before, whether the tube has been replaced, and whether the rim tape was ever changed. Repeat flats in the same wheel often trace back to rim tape that has shifted, a spoke end poking through, or a patch that no longer seals.

Bring the parts, not just the bike

If you have already swapped the tube yourself, bring the old one. A tube with a hole in it is direct evidence: the position of the hole tells us whether the cause was the tread, the rim, the valve, or a pinch between tire and rim. Bring the pump you normally use as well if you suspect it is not seating on the valve properly.

How to describe it at the counter

One or two sentences are enough. For example: "Rear wheel, loses all air overnight, third time this month, new tube fitted two weeks ago, nothing visible in the tread." That gives us the wheel, the speed of the leak, the pattern, and what you have already tried.

If you are unsure which tire your bike takes, the markings on the sidewall answer it, and we cover reading those separately.

What happens at the workshop

We repair bicycle tire punctures and inspect tires at our workshop, so the inspection starts with the notes you bring. Bring the bike in and describe when the air loss occurs, and we will work from there.
